newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan denies Uzbek charge of aiding Afghan war.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan denies Uzbek charge of aiding Afghan war.

text.p: Pakistan on Thursday rejected a charge by Uzbek President Islam Karimov that it was prolonging the civil war in Afghanistan by aiding the purist Taleban Islamic militia.

"We would express our regrets that he made such a statement," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said, referring to Karimov's speech on Wednesday at a two-day transport summit of the 10-nation Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) in Ashgabat, capital of Turkmenistan.
"We have no favourites in Afghanistan," the Pakistani spokesman said.

He said Pakistan had been making serious efforts for an intra-Afghan dialogue under the auspices of the United Nations or the 54-nation Organisation of the Islamic Conference to find a settlement on the formation of a broad-based government acceptable to all factions in the war-shattered country.

"Making allegations of this kind will only lead to a vitiation of the atmosphere," said the spokesman, whose country played host to most Afghan guerrilla groups who fought Soviet occupation of their country in the 1980s.

The Taleban government, which controls the capital Kabul and more than two-thirds of Afghanistan, was not invited to the ECO summit, where the country was represented by ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani.

The Pakistani spokesman said Islamabad's view was that Rabbani's government, ousted from Kabul last September and now based in opposition-controlled northern Afghanistan, was no longer the legitimate government of Afghanistan."
Karimov, while asking Pakistan to stop supporting the Taleban, said in his speech that the Afghan war was blocking resource-rich but landlocked central Asia's route to international markets.

Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, who returned to Islamabad overnight after attending the Ashgabat summit, told reporters on Thursday that ECO transport projects could not materialise without a return of peace in Afghanistan.
"Everybody should sit at the table," he said, urging the warring Afghan factions to settle their differences in talks.
